1.title: A Pond in Spring
paras: A pond is full of life in spring. Frogs lay spawn, a clump of jelly with many tiny eggs. Tall reeds, grassy plants that grow in wet places, sway at the edge. A snapping turtle lurks there, which means it waits quietly out of sight.

Under the water live dragonfly nymphs, young dragonflies that cannot fly yet. Later they emerge, which means they come out of the water, and climb up a stem. A muskrat is a furry animal that swims and eats water plants. Turtles bask, or lie in the warm sun, on a log. Early in the morning, before the wind comes up, the pond is serene, which means calm and peaceful.

1.title: Bats at Night
paras: Most bats are nocturnal, which means they are awake at night. In the day they sleep in a roost, a place where bats rest together. At dusk, the time just after the sun goes down, they fly out to hunt.

Many bats hunt by echolocation, finding things by listening to echoes. They devour, or eat hungrily, moths and beetles. A bat's wing is a membrane, a thin, stretchy skin, between long finger bones. A mother bat feeds her pup, a baby bat, with milk. In winter, some bats hibernate, or sleep deeply until spring.

1.title: The Weather Watcher
paras: A meteorologist is a scientist who studies the weather. Each day she makes a forecast, a report that tells what the weather will probably be. Today she says there will be drizzle, light rain with very small drops. A gust, a sudden, strong rush of wind, may shake the trees.

In winter, cold air can bring sleet, rain that freezes into tiny bits of ice. A blizzard is a snowstorm with strong winds. In summer, humid air, air with a lot of water in it that you cannot see, feels sticky. A drought, a long time with little or no rain, can dry up streams.

1.title: How Bread Is Made
paras: Bread begins on a farm. Farmers grow wheat for its kernels, the small seeds of the plant. A mill, a building with machines that grind grain, turns them into flour.

A baker mixes the flour with water and yeast, tiny living things that help bread rise. This makes dough, a soft, thick mix that will become bread. She kneads it, which means she presses and folds it. It sits in a warm place until it swells, or gets bigger. Then she shapes a loaf, one big piece of bread, and bakes it. In the oven the crust, the hard outside of the bread, turns brown.

1.title: Helpers in Our Town
paras: Many people help a town run. When someone calls 911, a dispatcher, a person who answers emergency calls, sends help. A paramedic, a worker who gives medical care on the way to the hospital, rides in the ambulance. A pharmacist is a person who prepares and gives out medicine.

At school, the custodian, a worker who cleans and cares for the building, fixes a squeaky door. If a pipe leaks, a plumber comes to fix it. A surveyor, a worker who measures land, marks where a new road will go. An electrician is a worker who fixes wires and lights. A veterinarian is an animal doctor. At a meeting, the town council, a group of leaders who make the town's rules, thanks them all.

1.title: The Night Sky
paras: An astronomer is a scientist who studies stars and planets. She looks through a telescope, a tool that makes faraway things look closer. She finds a constellation, a group of stars that makes a shape. All these stars are part of our galaxy, a huge group of billions of stars.

A meteor is a streak of light made by a space rock burning up in the air. A comet, a ball of ice and dust, can grow a long, glowing tail. The Moon orbits Earth, which means it travels in a path around it. The Moon's surface has many craters, round holes made when rocks hit it.

1.title: Seeds and Blossoms
paras: A bean seed lies in the soil. When it gets water, it germinates, which means it starts to grow. Soon a seedling, a very young plant, pokes up. Its roots take in nutrients, things that help living things grow. Without water, the little plant would wilt, or droop and go limp.

In spring, an apple tree is covered with blossoms, flowers on a tree or bush. Inside them is nectar, a sweet liquid that bees drink. Bees also carry pollen, a fine powder made by flowers, from flower to flower. One day, an apple seed may grow into a sapling, a young tree.

1.title: In the Workshop
paras: Grandpa Luis builds a birdhouse in his workshop. First he puts on goggles, special glasses that keep his eyes safe. He cuts the wood and rubs it with sandpaper, rough paper that makes wood smooth. A clamp, a tool that holds pieces tightly together, keeps the glued sides still.

He uses a chisel, a tool with a sharp, flat edge, to carve a star on the front. He taps it with a mallet, a hammer with a wooden head. He bends a wire hook with pliers, a tool for gripping and bending. Then he holds up a level, a tool that shows if something is straight across, not tilted, to check the floor. A wrench, a tool for turning bolts, tightens the stand.

2.title: Life in the Desert
paras: A desert is arid, not wet. Some years it gets almost no rain. During the day the sand is scorching, but at night it is cool. Water is scarce there, not easy to find. There are few rivers or ponds. Even so, many plants and animals have ways to live there.

Many desert plants are succulents, such as cactuses and aloe. Reptiles, such as lizards, snakes, and tortoises, hide in the shade at noon. A tortoise moves in a sluggish way, not quickly. Desert rodents, such as mice and kangaroo rats, dig holes under the sand. Predators, such as hawks and coyotes, live there too. Many desert animals stay in the shade or underground when the sun is high. They come out in the evening, when the air is cooler. Their bodies and habits help them live with little water.

2.title: At the Farmers Market
paras: On Saturday, Ana and her dad go to the farmers market. Unlike the quiet library next door, the market is bustling. People walk from table to table with bags and baskets. The air smells of flowers and warm bread. Farmers sell produce, such as apples, carrots, and corn. The tomatoes are plump, not thin and wrinkled.

One table sells legumes, like beans, peas, and peanuts. Another sells dairy foods, such as milk, cheese, and yogurt. Ana smells herbs, such as basil and mint. The baker says that yesterday's bread is stale, but today's loaves are soft and fresh. Dad carries the glass jars of honey with care because they are fragile, not strong. Ana and her dad buy six tomatoes, a bag of carrots, and some cheese. They pay the farmers and say thank you. At home, they cook a big pot of soup.

2.title: Animals in Winter
paras: Winter is a hard time for animals. The days are brief, not long, and the nights are cold. Many waterfowl, such as ducks and geese, fly to warmer places. Some animals migrate too, like the humpback whales that swim to warm seas and the monarch butterflies that fly to Mexico. Animals must find ways to stay warm and find food.

Other animals stay. Mammals, such as foxes, deer, and rabbits, grow thicker coats. Birds fluff up their feathers to trap warm air. A rabbit's winter fur is dense, not thin. A chipmunk is drowsy most of the winter, not wide awake. It wakes up now and then to eat seeds it stored in the fall. Evergreens, such as pines and spruces, grow in the snowy woods. Maple trees are dormant in winter, but in spring they are busy growing again. When the snow melts, the woods fill with life.

targets.clue: the humpback whales that swim to warm seas and the monarch butterflies that fly to Mexico

targets.meaning: animals with fur or hair, like foxes

2.title: Our Solar System
paras: Our solar system has eight planets. Jupiter is colossal, not small. More than a thousand Earths could fit inside it. Neptune is frigid, not warm, because it is so far from the Sun. On some clear evenings, Venus is visible, not hidden, after sunset. Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun. Saturn has bright rings made of ice and rock. It takes Earth one year to travel around the Sun.

Space is full of interesting things. Many planets have satellites, such as our Moon and the moons of Mars. Astronauts wear gear, like helmets, gloves, and air tanks. Space debris, such as bolts, paint chips, and broken rocket parts, circles Earth. Rovers on Mars send back data, like photos and temperatures. Unlike Earth, which is full of plants and animals, Mars is barren. Scientists hope people will visit Mars one day.

targets.clue: our Moon and the moons of Mars

targets.meaning: things you wear for a job

targets.clue: bolts, paint chips, and broken rocket parts

2.title: Building a House
paras: Building a house takes many steps. It can take months of hard work. First, the land must be level, not bumpy. Machinery, like bulldozers and cranes, moves dirt and lifts heavy loads. Workers pour concrete for the floor. Wet concrete is soft, but dry concrete is rigid.

Next come the walls. Then workers add a roof to keep out rain and snow. Builders use materials, such as wood, bricks, and glass. The old shed out back was flimsy, but the new walls are strong. On the roof, workers must be cautious, not careless. Plumbers put in pipes for water. Electricians add wires for lights. Later, appliances, such as a stove, a refrigerator, and a washing machine, are put in. Last, the family brings furnishings, such as beds, sofas, and tables. Then the house is ready, and the family moves in.

targets.clue: a stove, a refrigerator, and a washing machine

2.title: Ocean Life
paras: The ocean is home to many kinds of life. The ocean covers most of Earth's surface. Near the beach the water is shallow, but far out it is very deep. Scientists study marine animals, such as whales, sharks, and sea stars. Crustaceans, such as crabs, lobsters, and shrimp, are often caught for food. Ocean water is salty, so people cannot drink it.

Scientists also study mollusks, like clams, snails, and octopuses. Many jellyfish are transparent, unlike crabs, which you cannot see through. A sea turtle is graceful in the water but clumsy on land. Some sharks are solitary, but sardines swim in big groups. Seabirds, such as gulls and pelicans, catch fish near the shore. Whales come up to the surface to breathe air. Some animals live so deep that sunlight never reaches them. Scientists still find new kinds of ocean animals every year.

targets.meaning: birds that live by the sea

2.title: Kinds of Weather
paras: Weather changes from day to day. One day may be warm and bright, and the next may be cold and wet. Clouds can be white, gray, or almost black. Some days are overcast, not sunny. We get precipitation, such as rain, snow, and hail. A spring day is often mild, not very hot or very cold. In summer, many days are hot. In winter, many days are cold.

Some storms are severe, like tornadoes and hurricanes. In a storm, the wind can be fierce, not gentle. The thunder can be deafening, not quiet. Lightning can flash across the sky. When a storm is near, it is safest to stay indoors. People wear outerwear, such as raincoats and boots, to stay dry. Scientists use instruments, like thermometers and rain gauges. They use what they learn to tell us what the weather may be like tomorrow.

2.title: At the Fire Station
paras: Our class visited the fire station. A firefighter named Mr. Ortiz showed us around. Firefighters help in emergencies, such as fires and car crashes. They must always be alert, not sleepy, even at night. When an alarm rings, they move in a swift way, not slowly. They can get dressed and be on the truck in about a minute.

They put on protective clothes, such as helmets, boots, and thick coats. The truck holds equipment, like hoses, ladders, and axes. The truck is long and red. We even got to sit in the driver's seat. Its siren is shrill, not soft and low. Other vehicles, such as ambulances and police cars, may come too. Back at the station, the floors are spotless, not messy. Mr. Ortiz told us to have a fire plan at home. We should know two ways out of every room.

3.title: The Big Storm
paras: Last spring, a big storm hit our town. I will never forget it. That morning, the air was tranquil. By noon, the wind was wild and loud. Dad looked at the barometer. It is a tool that helps tell when a storm is coming. We gathered provisions. We set out flashlights, batteries, and water.

Soon, rain fell in a deluge. It was a downpour that filled the streets. The thunder startled my little brother. It scared him, and he jumped. Right then, the power went out, so Mom lit a lantern. It is a light with a handle that you can carry. During the storm, I felt anxious. Later, when the sun came out, I felt calm again.
The next day, our yard was full of debris. We picked up branches, leaves, and pieces of a broken fence. It took us all morning to clean it up.

targets.clue: a tool that helps tell when a storm is coming

3.title: A Trip to the Aquarium
paras: Our class took a trip to the aquarium. It has many exhibits. There are giant tanks, touch pools, and a tunnel under the water. First we saw the shark tank. It was immense. It was so huge that a school bus could fit inside. Then a diver fed the stingrays. They are flat fish with long, thin tails.

The penguins were famished. They were so hungry that they gobbled up every fish. A moray eel stayed concealed in a rocky cave. A clownfish swam out in plain sight. The coral tank was vibrant. The tank of sand eels next to it looked dull and gray. Some of the fish were so small that we had to look closely to spot them.

At the gift shop, they sold souvenirs. We saw postcards, key chains, and stuffed sharks. Last, we saw a nautilus. It is a sea animal that lives in a spiral shell. It was the best field trip of the year.

targets.meaning: a sea animal with a shell

3.title: Grandma Rosa's Garden
paras: Grandma Rosa and I planted a garden. First, we added compost to the soil. It is a mix of old leaves and food scraps that helps plants grow. Then we dug a trench for the seeds. It is a long, narrow ditch. Grandma Rosa says good soil is the secret to a good garden.

All summer, we had to irrigate the garden. We watered it every morning before breakfast. Some intruders found our garden. Slugs, snails, and beetles chewed holes in the leaves. Pollinators came too. We saw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Grandma Rosa and I watched them for a long time.

The new bean leaves were tender. The old ones were tough. By August, the sunflowers were sturdy. They were strong enough to stand up in the wind. This year our beans were abundant. Last year, we picked only a few. We shared them with our neighbors.

targets.clue: a mix of old leaves and food scraps that helps plants grow

3.title: Inside a Beehive
paras: A beehive can hold thousands of bees. Honeybees live in a colony. It is a big group of animals that live together. The queen lays eggs in wax cells. They are tiny rooms with six sides. Worker bees are industrious. They are busy all day long. Some of them clean the hive, and others make wax.

A bee can detect flowers that are far away. It can sense them by their smell. In summer, flowers are plentiful. In winter, there are almost none. Outside, the winter air is frigid. Inside the hive, the bees huddle to stay warm. They take turns moving to the middle of the group.

Honey is made from the nectar that bees collect. It is one of many sweeteners. Others are sugar and maple syrup. Bees also have foes. Bears, skunks, and wasps attack hives. Beekeepers wear special suits and veils to keep from getting stung.

targets.clue: a big group of animals that live together

3.title: The Mail Carrier
paras: Ms. Kim is a mail carrier. Each morning, she drives through her territory. It is the area where she brings the mail. She carries parcels. They are boxes wrapped up to be sent by mail. She loads them into her truck before she leaves.

People send all kinds of correspondence. Letters, cards, and postcards fill her bag. On her way, she passes many vendors. A fruit stand, a taco truck, and a pretzel cart are on Main Street. She waves to them as she goes by.

Ms. Kim is always courteous. She is polite to everyone she meets. Her bag can be hefty. It is so heavy that her shoulder gets sore. Some summer days are sweltering. In winter, some days are freezing cold. Most addresses are legible. A few are so messy that she cannot read them. In the afternoon, she brings the outgoing mail back to the post office. Ms. Kim says her job helps people stay in touch.

3.title: Exploring Mars
paras: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. Mars is a desolate place. It is empty and quiet, with rocks and dust everywhere. Mars has many landforms. Mountains, valleys, and craters cover its surface. Olympus Mons, a volcano on Mars, is towering. Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth, is much shorter. Mars also has canyons. They are deep valleys with steep sides. Its soil is full of iron, which makes it look red. Mars has two small moons.

Nobody has walked on Mars yet. Scientists sent a rover to Mars. It is a robot car that drives over the rocky ground. It collects specimens. It scoops up bits of rock, dust, and soil. It also transmits photos. It sends them all the way to Earth. Scientists study the photos to learn about Mars. During a dust storm, the sky on Mars turns hazy. On a calm day, the sky is much clearer. Someday, people may visit Mars too.

targets.clue: a robot car that drives over the rocky ground
bits of rock, dust, and soil

3.title: How Crayons Are Made
paras: Crayons are made in a factory. A factory is a building where things are made by machines. First, workers melt paraffin. It is a kind of wax. They heat it until it is molten. It turns liquid, like warm syrup. Next, they stir in pigment. It is a powder that gives something its color.

Crayons come in many hues. There are reds, blues, greens, and more. The hot wax is poured into molds. At first, the wax is scalding. After a few minutes, it is cool enough to touch. Then a machine pushes the crayons out of the molds.

Workers inspect the crayons. They check for broken tips. A few crayons come out flawed. The good ones are perfect. Next, each crayon gets a paper label with the name of its color. Then the boxes go to many retailers. Some are toy stores, grocery stores, and big shops.

targets.clue: a powder that gives something its color
toy stores, grocery stores, and big shops

3.title: A Day at the Library
paras: On Saturday, Lily went to the library. The reading room was hushed. It was so quiet that she could hear pages turning. The library has many resources. There are books, computers, and magazines. Lily likes to read in a big, soft chair by the window.

Lily likes biographies. She reads books about Abraham Lincoln and Harriet Tubman. Today she was keen to find a book about whales. She was excited to learn about them. The librarian, Mr. Patel, showed her the catalog. It is a list of all the books in the library. She also found an atlas. It is a book of maps. She checked out three books.

Mr. Patel let her help with a job. Some old books were tattered. The new ones were neat and whole. One shelf was cluttered. The shelf next to it was tidy. Lily helped put the books in order. She can't wait to come back next week.

targets.clue: books about Abraham Lincoln and Harriet Tubman
a list of all the books in the library

texts.title: How a Butterfly Grows
paras: A butterfly changes as it grows. This big change is called metamorphosis. It begins as a tiny egg on a leaf. A larva, or caterpillar, hatches from the egg. It eats and eats.

Then the caterpillar forms a chrysalis, a hard case around its body. Inside, its body changes. At last, a butterfly comes out. It uses its antennae to smell and feel. It sips nectar from flowers through its proboscis, a long tube like a straw.

texts.title: Volcanoes
paras: A volcano is a place where melted rock comes up through the ground. Deep inside Earth, some rock is hot enough to melt. Melted rock under the ground is called magma. It rises through a vent, an opening in the ground.

When a volcano erupts, hot rock bursts out. Once melted rock reaches the surface, it is called lava. Lava is hot enough to burn trees. A volcano can also blast out ash, tiny bits of rock that fill the sky. At the top of many volcanoes is a crater, a bowl-shaped hole.

texts.title: Clouds and Rain
paras: Water is always moving between the ground and the sky. The sun warms lakes and oceans, and some water starts to evaporate. It turns into vapor, a gas we cannot see. The vapor rises into the atmosphere, the air around Earth.

High up, the air is cold, so the vapor starts to condense. It turns into tiny droplets that make clouds. When the droplets join and get heavy, they fall as precipitation, such as rain. In cold air, it falls as snow.

texts.title: Bones and Muscles
paras: A grown-up's body usually has 206 bones. Together they make the skeleton. It holds the body up and protects the soft parts inside. Your ribs are curved bones that protect your heart and lungs.

A joint is a place where two bones meet, like your knee or elbow. Smooth cartilage covers the ends of the bones so they can move easily. Bones cannot move on their own. A muscle pulls on a bone to move it. A muscle is joined to a bone by a strong cord called a tendon.

texts.title: Fossils
paras: A fossil is what is left of a plant or animal that lived long ago. Many fossils form in layers of sediment, such as mud and sand. Over a very long time, the layers press together and turn into rock. Sometimes a shell leaves an imprint, a shape pressed into the rock.

Tiny insects have been found trapped in amber, hardened tree sap. A paleontologist is a scientist who studies fossils. Fossils show us animals that are now extinct, such as the woolly mammoth. None of them are alive today.

texts.title: From Tree to Paper
paras: The paper in your notebook began as a tree. A logger cuts down trees and sends the logs to a paper factory. There, machines peel off the bark. Then they cut the wood into small chips.
The chips are cooked with water until they become pulp, a wet, mushy mix. The pulp is spread out, pressed flat, and dried to make paper. When you recycle paper, it can be made into new paper again.

texts.title: Our Moon
paras: The Moon is about one-fourth as wide as Earth. It travels in an orbit around Earth, a path it follows about once a month. As it moves, we see different shapes of its lit part. These shapes are called phases.

The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's, so things weigh less there. Its surface is covered with dust and round craters. In 1969, an astronaut named Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk there. His trip was the first lunar landing with people.

texts.title: Less Waste in Our Town
paras: Our town wants to make less waste. Each home gets a blue bin for paper, cans, and bottles. When we recycle these things, they are made into new things. Some plastic can be recycled too.
Food scraps and leaves go in a compost pile, where they break down into rich soil. Everything else goes to the landfill, a place where trash is buried in the ground.
